Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Pakistan is optimistic about the Obama administration's commitment to its region and will work with the United States on trying to root out extremism within its borders, Pakistan's foreign minister said. Pakistani Foreign Minister Makhdoom Shah Mehmood Qureshi meets U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Following a meeting with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Pakistani Foreign Minister Makhdoom Shah Mehmood Qureshi cited a "convergence of interests" between Washington and Islamabad and a "willingness to work together." "I see a lot of hope in the new administration, the new leadership, and Pakistan is willing to work with the American administration to fight extremism and terrorism," he said Tuesday. "We are determined to defeat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations." Qureshi is in Washington to take part in strategic review of U.S. policy to stabilize Afghanistan and neighboring Pakistan. The effort is being led by South Asian security expert Bruce Reidel and Ambassador Richard Holbrooke, U.S. special envoy. Afghan Foreign Minister Rangin D. Spanta also was leading a delegation from his country to take part in the review. He and Qureshi will meet with both Clinton and Holbrooke this week. U.S. President Barack Obama and Clinton tapped Holbrooke as special representative for the two countries, a signal of how the new administration considers Afghanistan and Pakistan intertwined in any solution to the war in Afghanistan and the terrorist threat along their shared border. "We are consulting very closely with the government of Pakistan on our strategic review of our way forward and I'm very grateful for the minister's advice and counsel," Clinton said after meeting with Qureshi. Last week Obama announced he is sending another 17,000 troops to Afghanistan to fight a strengthening insurgency, which Obama has called the "central front in our enduring struggle against terrorism and extremism." The troops will be sent to southern Afghanistan, which borders Pakistan and is a haven for Taliban insurgents. Pakistani officials have expressed concern the deployment will push the Taliban across the border into Pakistan and further destabilize their country. The Obama administration is conducting several reviews of U.S. policy in Afghanistan, including a review by Gen. David Petraeus, the commander in the region. Defense Secretary Robert Gates has said the original mission in Afghanistan was "too broad" and needs to be more "realistic and focused" for the United States to succeed. Pakistan is engaged in its own effort against Taliban militants in its Northwest Frontier Provence. The militants, who effectively control the country's Swat Valley, extended a cease-fire Tuesday as part of an agreement with the government, a deal the U.S. and NATO warn risks granting a safe haven to extremists near the Afghan border.  Watch why the deal is being viewed as a capitulation » . Swat Valley was once one of Pakistan's biggest tourist destinations. It is situated near the Afghanistan border and about 186 miles (300 kilometers) from Pakistan's capital, Islamabad. In recent months, militants have unleashed a wave of violence that has claimed hundreds of lives across the province. The militants want to require veils for women and beards for men and to ban music and television. The fighting has displaced nearly half of Swat's population, officials said. The central government has long exerted little control in the area, but it launched an intense military offensive in late July to flush out militants. As retaliation for the military presence, the Taliban carried out a series of deadly bombings, beheadings and kidnappings -- and said the attacks will continue until the troops pull out. The Taliban said Tuesday it was indefinitely extending a cease-fire Taliban leaders declared eight days ago after signing a controversial deal with the government to impose Islamic law, or Sharia, in the region. The Pakistani government's decision now to negotiate with Pakistan has been met with international criticism. Holbrooke has said the Obama administration was "troubled and confused" by the truce in Swat. Holbrooke and NATO officials have expressed concerns that such an accord could cede effective control of the Swat Valley to extremists.

Keywords: WASHINGTON, CNN, Pakistan

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — Pakistan is optimistic about the Obama administration’s commitment to the region and is prepared to work with the United States to root out extremism within its borders, the country’s foreign minister said.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Makhdoom Shah Mehmood Qureshi met with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Following the meeting, Qureshi cited a “convergence of interests” between Washington and Islamabad, as well as a “willingness to work together.”

“I see a lot of hope in the new administration, the new leadership, and Pakistan is willing to work with the American administration to fight extremism and terrorism,” he said Tuesday. “We are determined to defeat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations.”

Qureshi is in Washington to participate in a strategic review of U.S. policy aimed at stabilizing Afghanistan and neighboring Pakistan. The effort is being led by South Asian security expert Bruce Reidel and Ambassador Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. special envoy.

Afghan Foreign Minister Rangin D. Spanta is also leading a delegation from his country to participate in the review. He and Qureshi will meet with both Clinton and Holbrooke this week.

U.S. President Barack Obama and Clinton selected Holbrooke as special representative for the two countries, signaling that the new administration views Afghanistan and Pakistan as intertwined in any solution to the war in Afghanistan and the terrorist threat along their shared border.

“We are consulting very closely with the government of Pakistan on our strategic review of our way forward and I’m very grateful for the minister’s advice and counsel,” Clinton said after meeting with Qureshi.

Last week, Obama announced that he is sending an additional 17,000 troops to Afghanistan to combat a strengthening insurgency, which he has called the “central front in our enduring struggle against terrorism and extremism.”

The troops will be deployed to southern Afghanistan, which borders Pakistan and serves as a haven for Taliban insurgents. Pakistani officials have expressed concern that the deployment will push the Taliban across the border into Pakistan, further destabilizing the country.

The Obama administration is conducting several reviews of U.S. policy in Afghanistan, including one led by Gen. David Petraeus, the commander in the region. Defense Secretary Robert Gates has said that the original mission in Afghanistan was “too broad” and must become more “realistic and focused” for the United States to succeed.

Pakistan is pursuing its own campaign against Taliban militants in its Northwest Frontier Province. The militants, who effectively control the country’s Swat Valley, extended a cease-fire Tuesday as part of an agreement with the government—a deal that the United States and NATO warn could grant extremists a safe haven near the Afghan border.

Watch why the deal is being viewed as a capitulation ».

Swat Valley was once one of Pakistan’s leading tourist destinations. It lies near the Afghan border, about 186 miles (300 kilometers) from Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad.

In recent months, militants have unleashed a wave of violence that has claimed hundreds of lives across the province. They seek to require women to wear veils and men to grow beards, while banning music and television.

The fighting has displaced nearly half of Swat’s population, officials said. The central government has long exercised little control over the area, but in late July it launched an intense military offensive to drive out the militants.

In retaliation for the military presence, the Taliban carried out a series of deadly bombings, beheadings and kidnappings—and said the attacks would continue until the troops withdrew.

On Tuesday, the Taliban announced that it was extending indefinitely a cease-fire its leaders had declared eight days earlier after signing a controversial agreement with the government to impose Islamic law, or Sharia, in the region.

The Pakistani government’s decision to negotiate with Pakistan has drawn international criticism. Holbrooke has said the Obama administration was “troubled and confused” by the truce in Swat. He and NATO officials have expressed concern that such an accord could effectively cede control of the Swat Valley to extremists.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Pakistan’s foreign minister said his country is encouraged by the Obama administration’s attention to the region and is prepared to cooperate with the United States in eliminating extremism inside Pakistan.

After talks with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Pakistani Foreign Minister Makhdoom Shah Mehmood Qureshi said Islamabad and Washington share common goals and are ready to collaborate.

“The new administration and its leadership give me considerable hope, and Pakistan is prepared to join the American administration in combating terrorism and extremism,” Qureshi said Tuesday. He added that Pakistan was committed to defeating terrorism “in all its forms and manifestations.”

Qureshi traveled to Washington to participate in a strategic assessment of U.S. efforts to bring stability to Afghanistan and neighboring Pakistan. The review is being directed by South Asia security specialist Bruce Reidel and Ambassador Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. special envoy.

Afghan Foreign Minister Rangin D. Spanta was also heading a delegation from Afghanistan involved in the process. Both Spanta and Qureshi were scheduled to hold meetings with Clinton and Holbrooke during the week.

President Barack Obama and Clinton appointed Holbrooke as the special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan. The move reflected the administration’s view that the two countries are inseparable when addressing both the Afghan war and the terrorist danger along their common frontier.

Following her meeting with Qureshi, Clinton said the United States was coordinating closely with Pakistan’s government as it reviewed its future strategy. She also expressed appreciation for the foreign minister’s guidance and recommendations.

A week earlier, Obama announced that an additional 17,000 U.S. troops would be deployed to Afghanistan to confront a growing insurgency. He described Afghanistan as the “central front in our enduring struggle against terrorism and extremism.”

The reinforcements were to be stationed in southern Afghanistan, an area bordering Pakistan that provides refuge to Taliban fighters. Pakistani authorities have voiced fears that the added military pressure could drive Taliban militants over the border, worsening instability inside Pakistan.

The Obama administration was undertaking several examinations of American policy in Afghanistan. One was being conducted by Gen. David Petraeus, the U.S. commander responsible for the region.

Defense Secretary Robert Gates said the initial objectives in Afghanistan had been overly expansive and that the United States would need a narrower, more practical mission to achieve success.

At the same time, Pakistan was carrying out its own campaign against Taliban militants in the Northwest Frontier Province. The fighters, who held effective control over the Swat Valley, extended a cease-fire Tuesday under an agreement with the Pakistani government. The United States and NATO cautioned that the arrangement could give extremists a sanctuary close to Afghanistan’s border, and some viewed the deal as a surrender to the militants.

Once among Pakistan’s leading tourist destinations, the Swat Valley lies near Afghanistan and approximately 186 miles, or 300 kilometers, from Islamabad, the Pakistani capital.

During the preceding months, militants had launched widespread violence throughout the province, killing hundreds of people. They sought to make veils mandatory for women, require men to grow beards, and outlaw television and music.

Officials said the conflict had forced almost half of Swat’s residents from their homes. Although Pakistan’s central government had historically maintained limited authority in the region, it began a major military operation in late July aimed at driving the militants out.

In response to the deployment of government forces, the Taliban conducted deadly bombings, kidnappings and beheadings. The group warned that its attacks would persist until the troops withdrew.

On Tuesday, the Taliban announced that it was extending the cease-fire indefinitely. Taliban leaders had initially declared the truce eight days earlier after reaching a disputed agreement with the government to establish Islamic law, known as Sharia, in the area.

Pakistan’s decision to negotiate over the region drew criticism internationally. Holbrooke said the Obama administration was “troubled and confused” by the Swat cease-fire. He and NATO representatives warned that the agreement might effectively hand control of the valley to extremist forces.

Pakistan and the United States are seeking to strengthen cooperation through a broad review of regional policy and a series of high-level diplomatic discussions. The effort is focused on combating violent extremism, improving security in Pakistan, and creating the conditions for long-term stability in Afghanistan. Under the Obama administration, Washington has increasingly treated the challenges facing the two countries as part of a single regional problem rather than as separate conflicts.

American officials have emphasized that instability along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border allows militant organizations to operate across national boundaries, threaten local governments, and plan attacks beyond the region. As a result, the United States is consulting closely with Pakistani leaders while reassessing its political, military, and economic strategy. The review is intended to produce a coordinated approach that combines counterterrorism operations with stronger governance, economic development, and support for civilian institutions.

Pakistan, for its part, has reaffirmed its commitment to fighting terrorism and extremism. Pakistani officials argue that their country has suffered heavily from militant violence and has a direct national interest in restoring order. They have also stressed that lasting progress will require sustained international support, respect for Pakistan’s sovereignty, and policies that address the social and economic conditions in which extremist groups can gain influence.

The high-level talks reflect a stated convergence of interests. Both governments want to prevent Afghanistan from again becoming a base for international terrorist organizations, curb militant activity in Pakistan’s border regions, and reduce the danger that violence will spread across the region. They also recognize that military force alone cannot provide a durable solution. Effective cooperation will therefore need to include intelligence sharing, diplomatic engagement, economic assistance, reconstruction, and measures designed to strengthen public confidence in government.

Important differences remain, including disagreements over operational priorities, regional relationships, and the pace and scope of counterterrorism efforts. Mutual distrust has also complicated earlier attempts at cooperation. Nevertheless, the renewed dialogue suggests that both sides are prepared to build a more sustained partnership.

The central message emerging from the policy review and talks is that the security of Afghanistan, Pakistan, and the United States is interconnected. Progress in one country is unlikely to last if instability continues in the other. Pakistan’s public commitment to confronting terrorism, together with the Obama administration’s emphasis on regional coordination, therefore signals the possibility of closer and more comprehensive cooperation.

counterfactuals.output:
### Pakistan pledges cooperation with Obama administration against extremism

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Pakistan is prepared to work closely with the Obama administration in combating extremism, Pakistani Foreign Minister Shah Mehmood Qureshi said following talks with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

The meeting focused on security along Pakistan’s border with Afghanistan, the threat posed by militant groups and efforts to strengthen relations between Washington and Islamabad.

Qureshi said Pakistan recognized that terrorism and extremism posed a direct threat not only to the United States and Afghanistan, but also to Pakistan itself. He emphasized that Islamabad wanted a broader partnership with Washington that included economic development, democratic institutions and assistance for communities vulnerable to militant influence.

Clinton reaffirmed the importance of Pakistan as a U.S. partner and stressed the need for sustained cooperation against al Qaeda, the Taliban and other extremist organizations operating in the region.

Relations between the two countries have at times been strained by U.S. concerns over militant safe havens inside Pakistan and Pakistani anger over American missile strikes near the Afghan border. Pakistani officials have argued that military action alone cannot defeat extremism and have called for greater investment in education, jobs and infrastructure.

The discussions came as the Obama administration reviewed U.S. strategy in Afghanistan and Pakistan, with officials increasingly treating instability in the two countries as interconnected.

Qureshi said Pakistan was willing to coordinate with Washington but maintained that any joint approach should respect Pakistan’s sovereignty and recognize the political and economic pressures facing its civilian government.

Both sides described the talks as constructive and indicated that further high-level discussions were expected.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on U.S.-Pakistan relations under the newly inaugurated Obama administration, including the Afghanistan-Pakistan strategic review, the deployment of 17,000 additional U.S. troops, and concerns about Taliban activity in the Swat Valley.
counterfactuals.output:
## U.S.–Pakistan Relations in the Opening Weeks of the Obama Administration  
**Situation report: February 2009**

Relations between Washington and Islamabad remain strategically vital but strained as President Barack Obama begins reshaping U.S. policy toward Afghanistan and Pakistan. The administration views insurgent sanctuaries in Pakistan’s border regions as inseparable from the war in Afghanistan, while Pakistan’s government remains concerned about sovereignty, civilian casualties from U.S. drone strikes, and an American policy it believes has often emphasized military operations over economic and political stability.

### Afghanistan–Pakistan strategic review

President Obama has ordered a broad review of U.S. strategy in Afghanistan and Pakistan, led by former CIA official Bruce Riedel. The review is expected to examine:

- How to disrupt al-Qaeda and Taliban networks operating on both sides of the Afghanistan–Pakistan border.
- Whether U.S. military objectives in Afghanistan should be narrowed and clarified.
- How to strengthen Pakistan’s civilian government and security institutions.
- The proper balance among military action, development assistance, diplomacy, and regional cooperation.
- Pakistan’s security concerns regarding India, which influence where Islamabad deploys its forces and how it prioritizes militant threats.

The appointment of Richard Holbrooke as special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan underscores the administration’s intention to treat the two countries as a connected strategic theater. During regional consultations, U.S. officials have stressed that Pakistan is a partner rather than merely a staging ground for Afghan operations. Islamabad, however, is wary that the new approach could bring greater pressure to confront militants in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas and elsewhere.

### Deployment of 17,000 additional U.S. troops

On February 17, Obama authorized the deployment of approximately **17,000 additional U.S. troops to Afghanistan**, including an Army brigade and a Marine expeditionary force. The reinforcement, part of a larger request from U.S. commanders, is intended primarily to improve security in southern and eastern Afghanistan ahead of the August presidential election and to counter a growing Taliban insurgency.

The decision has direct implications for Pakistan:

- Additional U.S. troops may push insurgents toward sanctuaries across the Pakistani border.
- The deployment will likely increase pressure on Pakistan’s army and Frontier Corps to interdict Taliban movements and supply networks.
- U.S. and NATO forces remain dependent on supply routes through Pakistan, making political stability and cooperation with Islamabad essential.
- Pakistani officials may resist any expansion of unilateral U.S. action on their territory, particularly drone strikes, which are deeply unpopular among the public.

The troop deployment precedes completion of the broader strategic review, suggesting that the administration considers the deteriorating security situation too urgent to await a final policy framework.

### Taliban activity and the Swat Valley agreement

Washington is especially concerned about developments in the **Swat Valley**, where militants led by Maulana Fazlullah have challenged government authority, attacked schools—particularly girls’ schools—and imposed harsh social restrictions.

In mid-February, the provincial government in Pakistan’s North-West Frontier Province reached an agreement with representatives of the Tehrik-e-Nifaz-e-Shariat-e-Mohammadi movement. The arrangement calls for the introduction of a form of Islamic law in Swat and the wider Malakand region in exchange for a ceasefire.

Pakistani authorities portray the agreement as a locally negotiated peace initiative that could separate reconcilable militants from hard-line insurgents. U.S. officials and other critics fear it may instead:

- Legitimize Taliban authority.
- Reward militants for using violence.
- Allow fighters time to regroup and rearm.
- Create a sanctuary beyond effective government control.
- Encourage similar movements elsewhere in Pakistan.

The Swat situation is particularly troubling because the valley lies outside the tribal belt and relatively close to major population centers. Taliban gains there suggest that militant influence is no longer confined to remote areas along the Afghan border.

### Outlook

The Obama administration appears likely to combine increased military pressure in Afghanistan with expanded economic and civilian assistance to Pakistan. Proposals in Congress for substantial, long-term nonmilitary aid could help rebuild trust and strengthen Pakistan’s elected government. At the same time, Washington will demand measurable action against al-Qaeda, the Afghan Taliban, and Pakistani militant groups.

The central challenge is that the two countries’ priorities do not fully coincide. Washington regards cross-border militant sanctuaries as an immediate threat to Afghanistan and U.S. security. Pakistan continues to weigh that threat against domestic instability, hostility toward unilateral American operations, and its longstanding rivalry with India. The outcome of the strategic review—and whether the Swat ceasefire reduces violence or entrenches Taliban control—will be early tests of the new administration’s approach.

counterfactuals.output:
**Pakistan sees common ground with Washington in terrorism fight, Qureshi says**

**ISLAMABAD —** Pakistan sees a “convergence of interests” with the United States in combating terrorism and stabilizing the region, Foreign Minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi said, signaling Islamabad’s willingness to work closely with the new administration of President Barack Obama.

Qureshi’s statement came as Washington prepared to reassess its strategy toward Afghanistan and Pakistan, where militant groups had expanded their influence along the countries’ mountainous border. Pakistani officials said cooperation with the United States should extend beyond military operations to include economic development, stronger civilian institutions and efforts to address the causes of extremism.

The foreign minister welcomed early contact with Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and said the two governments shared an interest in defeating terrorism. At the same time, Pakistan has repeatedly stressed that its sovereignty must be respected, a reference to deep public anger over U.S. missile strikes against suspected militant targets inside Pakistani territory.

Clinton, in outlining the Obama administration’s approach, described Afghanistan and Pakistan as one of Washington’s most difficult foreign-policy challenges. She said veteran diplomat Richard Holbrooke would lead efforts to develop “a strategic and sustainable approach to this critical region.”

Holbrooke, best known for helping broker the Dayton peace accords that ended the Bosnian war, was appointed U.S. special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan. The title reflected the administration’s view that the insurgency in Afghanistan could not be addressed separately from militant sanctuaries, political instability and economic hardship in Pakistan.

His mandate was expected to involve extensive consultations with leaders in Islamabad and Kabul, as well as coordination with NATO allies, regional governments and international donors. Although India was not included in his formal title, Holbrooke’s work inevitably touched on wider South Asian tensions, particularly Pakistan’s concern that its security priorities could not be separated from its rivalry with New Delhi.

Pakistani leaders broadly welcomed the appointment but made clear they expected Holbrooke to take account of Islamabad’s security concerns and the political sensitivities surrounding American operations in the border region. Cooperation with Washington had become increasingly contentious as Pakistan battled militants at home while facing accusations that elements of the Taliban and other armed groups continued to find refuge on its soil.

Qureshi’s reference to a convergence of interests appeared intended to emphasize the common threat posed by al-Qaeda, the Taliban and affiliated organizations. Pakistan had suffered a series of bombings and assassinations, including the killing of former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto in December 2007, while the United States viewed the border region as central to the war in Afghanistan and the campaign against al-Qaeda.

Despite that shared threat, the relationship remained marked by mistrust. U.S. officials pressed Pakistan to act more decisively against militant networks, while Pakistani officials argued that Washington had relied too heavily on force and had failed to provide consistent long-term support.

Clinton and other Obama administration officials indicated that the new strategy would seek a broader partnership, combining security cooperation with diplomacy, development assistance and support for Pakistan’s civilian government. Qureshi said such an approach could provide the basis for a more durable relationship—one built not solely around short-term counterterrorism demands but around mutual regional interests.

Holbrooke’s regional role was therefore expected to test whether the two countries could translate their stated common objectives into coordinated policy. His immediate tasks included helping shape the administration’s Afghanistan-Pakistan review, improving often strained relations among Washington, Islamabad and Kabul, and encouraging more effective action against militant groups operating across the border.

counterfactuals.output:
# Pakistan optimistic over Obama’s regional policy

**ISLAMABAD, Feb. 19 —** Pakistan is optimistic that a U.S. review of policy toward Afghanistan and Pakistan under President Barack Obama will produce a broader regional strategy combining military action with diplomacy and economic development, Pakistani officials said.

Islamabad, a key U.S. counterterrorism partner, has long argued that militancy cannot be defeated by force alone. It wants Washington to address political grievances, poverty and weak government institutions while increasing support for Pakistan’s security forces and civilian administration.

The Obama administration is reviewing its approach to the region amid a worsening insurgency in Afghanistan and concern that al Qaeda and Taliban militants are using Pakistan’s border areas as safe havens. U.S. officials have signaled that Pakistan will be central to the new strategy.

Obama has also approved the deployment of about 17,000 additional U.S. troops to Afghanistan, reinforcing forces already fighting a resurgent Taliban. Pakistan says greater military pressure across the border must be accompanied by closer coordination to prevent militants from moving into Pakistani territory.

Relations between Washington and Islamabad have at times been strained by U.S. missile strikes inside Pakistan and allegations that elements of the Pakistani security establishment retain links with militant groups. Pakistan says it has paid a heavy price for supporting the campaign against terrorism, citing thousands of casualties from militant attacks and military operations.

At the same time, Islamabad has defended negotiations with Taliban militants in parts of the northwest, including a controversial agreement intended to restore peace in the Swat Valley through the introduction of Islamic law.

Critics in Pakistan and abroad say such deals risk legitimizing militants and allowing them time to regroup. Pakistani officials argue that negotiations are aimed at isolating reconcilable fighters from hard-line militants and that force remains an option against groups that reject the authority of the state.

Washington has said it is watching the talks closely and has stressed that any agreement must end violence rather than create new militant sanctuaries.

Pakistani officials hope the U.S. policy review will recognize the distinction between local insurgents who may be brought into the political process and transnational groups linked to al Qaeda. They also want greater international aid for border regions where unemployment, displacement and poor public services have helped militants gain influence.

The review is expected to shape U.S. policy ahead of intensified operations in Afghanistan. Islamabad says a durable solution will require cooperation among Pakistan, Afghanistan and the United States, as well as sustained diplomatic engagement with other regional powers.
